newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Veba steps in as top Degussa shareholder.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Veba steps in as top Degussa shareholder.

text.p: German utility Veba AG said on Wednesday it had agreed to buy 36.4 percent of chemicals and metals firm Degussa AG in a strategic move seen boosting both companies' earnings prospects.

The Duesseldorf-based utility said it would pay 2.9 billion marks ($1.7 billion), or 86.80 marks per share, for a Degussa package held by GFC Gesellschaft fuer Chemiewerte mbH, owned by chemicals firm Henkel KGaA, Dresdner Bank AG and reinsurance group Munich Re.
Both firms' shares rallied on the news as analysts said the acquisition, which would make Veba Degussa's largest single shareholder, would give both companies a strong strategic partner.

The main point of the deal is to exploit synergies between Degussa and Veba's chemical unit Huels, both of which are trying to boost productivity and concentrate on core business to become more internationally competitive.

"I see the transaction as an opportunity to strengthen our chemicals activities," Veba's chief executive Ulrich Hartmann said. He told Reuters later that the utility giant had no current plans to increase its stake in Degussa.
"We feel very good about our new large shareholder," Degussa chief executive Uwe-Ernst Bufe said, noting that Degussa had a stronger international record than Veba.
"From Degussa's perspective, we are very confident that we can exploit our potential further and continue to increase our market value," he told Reuters.

Degussa's shares, which had closed on Tuesday at 76 marks, surged to end bourse trade up 8.80 marks, or 11.6 percent, at 84.80 marks while Veba was trading up 90 pfennigs at 99.70 marks, in line with the broader market.

Analysts gave the news a swift thumbs up. Degussa, with 26,000 staff and annual sales of chemicals, metals and health products of some 13.8 billion marks is seen as broadly compatible with Huels, which has sales of around 10 billion marks and 28,600 employees.
"I believe Veba wanted to have a major player in chemicals and what Degussa has achieved under Bufe has been quite impressive," said Bayerische Vereinsbank pharmaceuticals analyst Nasseer Panju.
"The fact that Veba took a 36 percent stake, when they could have easily brought it up to 51 percent over the market, is a sign they believe in the Degussa management," he said.

BHF Bank utilities analyst Thomas Deser raised Veba to a "buy" from "hold" on the news, which he saw as marking the end of Veba's restructuring phase and the start of an acquisition spree in other sectors, such as services and electricity.

Veba's Hartmann, who confirmed Veba was interested in more acquisitions, said Degussa could continue its activities in hydrogen peroxide, cyanide, and automotive catalyzers, among others, where it is among world leaders.
He said only around 15 percent of Veba's and Degussa's businesses overlapped so that no significant job cuts were to be expected as a result of the alliance.
Degussa's Bufe said it was too early to talk of any radical restructuring within the Degussa group. "But we will certainly also discuss our problem zones with Veba," he said.

Veba said it did not need to raise any new capital to finance the deal, from which Henkel, which owns 16.6 percent of Degussa, stands to earn 1.3 billion marks, while Dresdner and Muenchener Rueckversicherungs AG will each earn 789 million marks for their 9.9 percent stakes.

Veba's net profit rose 25 percent to 2.63 billion marks in 1996, and first quarter profits this year advanced seven percent after an unexpectedly strong start to the year, with sales up 7.8 percent at 19.624 billion marks.
Degussa reported a 20 percent rise in pre-tax profits for the first quarter of its 1996/1997 business year, having reported a sluggish two percent profit rise to 413 million marks for 1995/1996.
